answer.label: No ancient source for Pythagoras — an unsourced modern attribution
answer.authorDates: Credited to Pythagoras (c. 570 – c. 495 BC) only in modern quotation books
answer.sourceLine: No ancient text attributes this line to Pythagoras, who left no surviving writings. English Wikiquote ↗ cites only James Geary’s 2007 aphorism anthology, and Spanish Wikiquote ↗ cites only modern Spanish quotation dictionaries. Who first wrote it is unknown.

source.excerpt: Educate the children and it won’t be necessary to punish the men.
trail: English Wikiquote ↗ lists the line with only one source note: “As quoted in Geary’s Guide to the World’s Great Aphorists (2007) by James Geary.” It cites no ancient text.
Spanish Wikiquote ↗ gives the Spanish form and cites three modern Spanish quotation dictionaries, by Bartra, Señor and Palomo. It names no classical source.
The Golden Verses ↗, the best-known collection of Pythagorean maxims, has no line about educating children or punishing men. Wikipedia reproduces the full 71-line translation.
Wikipedia ↗ notes that “No authentic writings of Pythagoras have survived.” Any exact wording credited to him needs a later ancient witness, and this line has none.
source.excerptNote: The line is just as common in Spanish: “Educad a los niños y no será necesario castigar a los hombres.” Neither version comes with an ancient citation.
source.rightsNote: We could not trace this wording to any ancient text or named original author, so we make no copyright claim about it. James Geary’s 2007 anthology is itself a modern in-copyright book, but it is a place where the line was collected, not its origin.

author.name: Pythagoras
author.heading: About Pythagoras
author.bio: Pythagoras founded a school at Croton in southern Italy around 530 BC. Its members reportedly lived a communal, ascetic life and were sworn to secrecy. No authentic writings of Pythagoras have survived, and almost everything known about him comes from biographies written centuries after his death. That gap makes him one of the easiest names to hang an unsourced maxim on.

cite.sourceCitation: No ancient source known. Quoted as Pythagoras in James Geary, Geary’s Guide to the World’s Great Aphorists (Bloomsbury, 2007), as cited by Wikiquote, “Pythagoras.”

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Pythagoras
misattribution.intro: The saying circulates widely in English and Spanish as a maxim of Pythagoras. Every source we could trace is a modern quotation collection or a recent article. None is an ancient text.

items.who: Geary’s Guide to the World’s Great Aphorists
items.why: This is the only source that English Wikiquote ↗ gives for the line. It is a modern anthology, and Wikiquote names no ancient passage behind it.
Spanish Wikiquote ↗ cites only these modern dictionaries for “Educad a los niños y no será necesario castigar a los hombres.”
A Spanish article in El Cronista ↗ says the phrase is “incluida en Sentencias de oro” but gives no edition or verse. The full Golden Verses ↗ has no such line.
Graciousquotes ↗ files the line as “plausible” and points back to the Geary citation. It does not give an original text.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no ancient evidence that Pythagoras said this. No authentic writings of his survive ↗, the line is absent from the Golden Verses, and its only cited sources are modern quotation books. Who first wrote it is unknown.

context.heading: Why it sticks
lead: The line sounds like an ancient proverb: short, balanced, and morally tidy. It sits naturally beside the real Pythagorean emphasis on disciplined communal life, and that makes Pythagoras an easy name to attach. But Pythagoras left no surviving writings, so an exact maxim credited to him needs an ancient witness, such as a later biographer, an anthologist or the Golden Verses. This one has none.

In Spanish-speaking countries the saying is a staple of school posters and newspaper features. Those features often repeat the attribution without a source, or assign it to the Golden Verses, where it does not appear.
context.pull: An exact maxim credited to Pythagoras needs an ancient witness. This one has none.
